## Figure 12: Project Design

1. Rice is Thailand’s most important food crop, accounting for roughly half of the country’s agricultural land and employing 18 million smallholder farmers. However, rice farming is also a significant contributor to the country's greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, mainly through methane from paddy fields.
2. Smallholder rice farmers in Thailand are vulnerable to climate change due to changing rainfall patterns, as well as increasing frequency and severity of flooding and droughts.
3. The project will focus on promoting adaptation and mitigation results from the rice farming sector in Thailand. If approved, it will be the first GEF project to focus solely on transforming the rice sector into a more sustainable one by providing smallholder farmers with access to a suite of climate-smart technologies and practices, as well as farmer-friendly financial services.

From this perspective, the project's outcomes and outputs focus on the fundamental components that will enable the transformation towards a more sustainable and resilient productivity of Thailand’s rice farming (through climate-smart practices and technologies) and its adaptive capacity (through institutional strengthening, improved market conditions and mastery of climate change knowledge). With the launch of the global campaign of Clean Cooking Solution for all (CCSALL) initiated in 2013, the Government of Nepal had endorsed Investment Prospectus for clean cooking solutions [1] and Biomass Energy Strategy [2]. To mitigate the impacts of climate change and strengthen resilience of the most vulnerable communities to adapt to climate change, Alternative Energy Promotion Centre (AEP) has proposed to implement the project "Mitigating GHG emission through modern, efficient and climate friendly clean cooking solutions (CCS)". The project will be implemented in Nepal by AEP with financial support from the Green Climate Fund. It aims at mitigating climate change impacts on vulnerable communities of Nepal by: (i) Introducing innovative concepts in Nepal of (ii) bulk tendering via reverse auctioning for cost effectiveness; (iii) output based financing for de-risking of investments and (iv) mainstreaming and capacitating local governments to ensure long-term sustainability. The project will be implemented in 10 districts across the country up to now and could be game changers in the clean cooking sector.
